Section 2.1 — The Holy Character of God as the Ground of All Ethics

In the first unit we said that Christian ethics measures every action against God's own character. Now we must ask the obvious next question: what is that character, and why should it be the measure of anything? If you do not settle this, everything that follows will float free of its anchor. So let us put the anchor down deep. The ground of all ethics is the holiness of God — not a rule He keeps, but the very purity of who He is. "Be holy, for I am holy" (1 Peter 1:16, citing Leviticus). Notice the logic of that command. God does not say, be holy because holiness works, or because the community needs it. He says, be holy because I am. The reason for the standard is the nature of God Himself.

Let me give you a picture I have carried since boyhood. My father grew up on a farm, and in those days a farmer had to do his own carpentry, so for a few years he made his living as a carpenter. In our garage there were some very old tools, and one of them was a plumb line made of brass. It was a simple thing — a weight on a string — but it did one job perfectly: hung against a wall, gravity pulled it true, and it showed you at once whether the wall was straight. The plumb line does not argue and it does not flatter; it simply does not lie. When the Lord showed Amos a plumb line set in the midst of His people, that was the point. Ethics is not finally a matter of our preferences, our traditions, or how a thing looks from the outside. There is a standard, fixed and true, and it measures us whether we consent to it or not. The whole of Christian ethics begins here: not with what we feel is right, but with the straight line God Himself has set beside our lives.

This protects us from two ancient errors, and I want you to be able to name them, because your people will stumble into both. The first error says that things are good because God arbitrarily commands them — that He could have called murder righteous if He had chosen to, and good is simply whatever the Almighty happens to decree. That makes God a tyrant and goodness a coin-flip. The second error says that things are good by some standard above God, to which even He must bow — which makes God no longer God, but a servant of a higher law. The biblical answer slices cleanly between them: a thing is good because it reflects the unchanging character of God. Goodness is neither arbitrary nor above Him. It is Him, expressed. His commands are not random and they are not borrowed; they are the overflow of His own perfect nature.

From this single truth flows a principle we will lean on again and again in this course, one I have taught for years and built into our Systematic Theology: every human being is made in the image of God, and therefore every human being possesses a worth that cannot be earned, diminished, or revoked. "So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them" (Genesis 1:27). That worth does not rise and fall with a man's usefulness, his health, his morality, or his agreement with us. It is irreducible, because it is grounded not in him but in the God whose image he bears. Hold onto that. When we reach the sanctity of life, the treatment of the poor, and the discipline of the sinning brother, this is the principle we will be applying.

Cross-Reference · Systematic TheologyThe holiness and attributes of God, and the doctrine of man as image-bearer, are treated fully in the Systematic Theology course (Unit 2, The Doctrine of God; and Unit 5, The Doctrine of Man).
Section 2.2 — Law and Fulfillment: The Moral Law and the Coming of Christ

If God's character is the standard, the law is the place where that character was written down for us in words. God did not leave us to guess at His holiness. He built a moral order into the very creation, and then He stated it plainly at Sinai. The Ten Commandments are not ten arbitrary rules; they are a portrait of God's character translated into the shape of a human life — one God, no idols, His name honored, His day kept, and then the horizontal commands that protect life, marriage, property, truth, and the contented heart.

Conservative teachers have long found it useful to distinguish three strands within the law of Moses: the ceremonial law that governed sacrifice and temple, the civil law that ordered the nation of Israel, and the moral law that expresses God's unchanging will. The ceremonial pointed forward to Christ and is fulfilled in Him; the civil was given to a particular nation in a particular time; but the moral law, rooted in God's own nature, abides. This is why we still teach the Ten Commandments and no longer offer lambs. Learn this distinction well, because much confusion in the church comes from collapsing it — either binding people to laws Christ has fulfilled, or discarding moral commands that still stand.

Then came the Lord Jesus, and here a careful word is needed, for many imagine that He came to soften or set aside the law. He says the opposite. "Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to destroy but to fulfill" (Matthew 5:17). And in the Sermon on the Mount He does not lower the law's demand; He drives it inward to the heart. You have heard it said, do not murder — but I say, do not even nurse the anger that kills. You have heard, do not commit adultery — but I say, do not even harbor the lust that betrays. Christ takes the law off the surface of behavior and presses it down into the thoughts and intents, exactly where 2 Timothy told us the Word reaches. This is progressive revelation at its summit: not a new and contradictory standard, but the full unveiling of what the law always meant. The One who gave the law on the mountain now expounds it on another, and then goes to a third to fulfill its every demand in His own body.
Section 2.3 — Grace-Empowered Obedience and the Fruit of the Spirit

Now we arrive at the hinge of the whole Christian life, and if a man gets this wrong he will either despair or grow proud, and often both by turns. The question is this: once we see the law in all its inward, heart-searching demand, how can any of us hope to keep it? And the honest biblical answer is that, left to ourselves, we cannot. "There is none righteous, no, not one" (Romans 3:10). The law was never given as a ladder to climb to God. One of its great purposes is to be the mirror that shows us our filth and drives us, despairing of ourselves, to the cross. The law diagnoses; it cannot cure.

The cure is the gospel. In Christ, the demand of the law is satisfied and its penalty paid, and the believer is declared righteous as a free gift. But the gospel does not stop at the courtroom. The same grace that justifies also goes to work within, and here is the truth that rescues ethics from being a grim exercise in willpower: holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, not the achievement of the flesh. "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22–23). Mark the word — fruit, not works. Fruit is not manufactured by the branch gritting its teeth; it is borne as the life of the vine flows through it. Christian character is grown, by the Spirit, in a soul united to Christ.

This is why we held so firmly in Unit 1 to the order of grace before obedience, and why we will hold it all the way through. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we have been accepted, and therefore we obey, and the very power to obey is itself a gift. Get that order backward and you produce either a Pharisee or a wreck. Keep it straight and obedience becomes what it was always meant to be — not the anxious payment of a debt, but the glad response of a son to the Father who has already run down the road to embrace him.
Section 2.4 — Reading Scripture Rightly and Weighing the Ethical Systems

Two practical matters remain before we move into the work of ministry itself. The first is how to handle the Word so that we apply it rightly and do not twist it. We hold to what has been called the grammatical-historical method, which is a careful name for a humble practice: we ask what the human author, carried along by the Spirit, actually meant to say to his original readers, in the ordinary sense of his words and the setting of his time — and only then do we ask how that abiding truth bears on us. We do not make the text a mirror for our own preferences or a wax nose to be bent toward whatever we already wished to do. The pastor who proves his point by ripping a verse from its context has not honored the Word; he has used it. And a congregation trained by such handling will learn to do the same to one another. Read the verse in its paragraph, the paragraph in its book, and the book in the whole counsel of God.

The second matter is how to think about the ethical systems the world has built, which you studied in part in Unit 1. The philosophers have largely sorted themselves into three families: those who locate the good in character (the virtue traditions), those who locate it in duty and rule (the deontologists), and those who locate it in consequences (the various utilitarians). Here is the discerning Christian's verdict. Each of the three has hold of something real, and it is no accident, for each is borrowing from the moral order God actually built. Scripture cares about character — it is the whole point of the fruit of the Spirit. Scripture cares about duty — God issues commands and expects obedience. Scripture cares about consequences — love weighs the effect of its actions on a neighbor. The failure of each system is never that it sees nothing true; it is that it tears its one fragment loose from God and tries to make that fragment carry the whole weight of morality alone. The Christian does not choose one of the three and reject the others. He gathers up the truth in each — virtue, duty, and consequence — and orders all of it under the authority of God's revelation, where it finally belongs.

Cross-Reference · Doctrinal PreachingThe imago Dei principle (Section 2.1) and the grace-before-works order (Section 2.3) were both developed at length in the Doctrinal Preaching course (Unit 5, Preaching the Doctrine of Man; and Unit 8, Preaching the Doctrine of Salvation) and carry directly into the homiletics of this course.

mc.stem: 1. The unit grounds all ethics in the holiness of God, described as:
options: the very purity of who God is
a rule God chooses to keep
mc.why: Holiness is not a rule God keeps but the very purity of who He is.

es_reference.stem: 1. La unidad fundamenta toda ética en la santidad de Dios, descrita como:
options: la pureza misma de quien Dios es
una regla que Dios escoge guardar
es_reference.why: La santidad no es una regla que Dios guarda sino la pureza misma de quien Él es.

mc.stem: 2. “Be holy, for I am holy” teaches that the reason for the moral standard is:
mc.why: God commands holiness because of who He is; the reason for the standard is His own nature.

es_reference.stem: 2. «Sed santos, porque yo soy santo» enseña que la razón de la norma moral es:
options: la utilidad de la vida santa
es_reference.why: Dios manda la santidad por causa de quien Él es; la razón de la norma es su propia naturaleza.

mc.stem: 3. The biblical answer between the two ancient errors is that a thing is good because:
options: it reflects the unchanging character of God
mc.why: Goodness is neither arbitrary nor above God; a thing is good because it reflects His unchanging character.

es_reference.stem: 3. La respuesta bíblica entre los dos errores antiguos es que una cosa es buena porque:
options: refleja el carácter inmutable de Dios
Dios pudo haber decretado lo contrario
es_reference.why: La bondad no es ni arbitraria ni superior a Dios; una cosa es buena porque refleja su carácter inmutable.

mc.stem: 4. Genesis 1:27 is cited to ground the principle that every human being possesses:
options: worth that cannot be earned or revoked
mc.why: Because all bear God's image, every person has worth that cannot be earned, diminished, or revoked.

es_reference.stem: 4. Génesis 1:27 se cita para fundamentar el principio de que todo ser humano posee:
options: un valor que no puede ganarse ni revocarse
es_reference.why: Porque todos llevan la imagen de Dios, toda persona tiene un valor que no puede ganarse, disminuirse ni revocarse.

mc.stem: 5. A person's irreducible worth is grounded not in him but in:
options: the God whose image he bears
mc.why: Worth does not rise and fall with usefulness or morality; it is grounded in the God whose image he bears.

es_reference.stem: 5. El valor irreducible de una persona está fundado no en ella sino en:
es_reference.why: El valor no sube ni baja con la utilidad ni la moralidad; está fundado en el Dios cuya imagen lleva.

mc.stem: 6. The Ten Commandments are described as:
options: a portrait of God's character in the shape of a human life
mc.why: They are not arbitrary rules but God's character translated into the shape of a human life.

es_reference.stem: 6. Los Diez Mandamientos se describen como:
options: un retrato del carácter de Dios en la forma de una vida humana
ley civil para las naciones modernas
es_reference.why: No son reglas arbitrarias sino el carácter de Dios traducido a la forma de una vida humana.

mc.stem: 7. Which strand of the law, rooted in God's own nature, is said to abide?
mc.why: Ceremonial and civil were for a time and a nation; the moral law, rooted in God's nature, abides.

es_reference.stem: 7. ¿Cuál hebra de la ley, arraigada en la naturaleza misma de Dios, se dice que permanece?
es_reference.why: La ceremonial y la civil fueron para un tiempo y una nación; la ley moral, arraigada en la naturaleza de Dios, permanece.

mc.stem: 8. In Matthew 5:17, Jesus says He came not to destroy the Law but to:
mc.why: Christ did not come to abolish or soften the law but to fulfill it.

es_reference.stem: 8. En Mateo 5:17, Jesús dice que vino no para abrogar la ley sino para:
es_reference.why: Cristo no vino a abolir ni suavizar la ley sino a cumplirla.

mc.stem: 9. In the Sermon on the Mount, Christ handles the law by:
options: driving it inward to the heart
mc.why: He does not lower the law's demand; He drives it inward to the thoughts and intents of the heart.

es_reference.stem: 9. En el Sermón del Monte, Cristo maneja la ley:
es_reference.why: No rebaja la exigencia de la ley; la impulsa hacia adentro, a los pensamientos e intenciones del corazón.

mc.stem: 10. The unit describes Christ's exposition of the law as the summit of:
mc.why: It is progressive revelation at its summit: the full unveiling of what the law always meant.

es_reference.stem: 10. La unidad describe la exposición de la ley por Cristo como la cúspide de:
es_reference.why: Es la revelación progresiva en su cúspide: el pleno develamiento de lo que la ley siempre significó.

mc.stem: 11. Romans 3:10 (“none righteous”) is used to teach that, left to ourselves, we:
options: may keep part of the law
mc.why: Left to ourselves we cannot keep the law; it was never a ladder to climb to God.

es_reference.stem: 11. Romanos 3:10 («no hay justo») se usa para enseñar que, dejados a nosotros mismos:
options: podemos guardar parte de la ley
es_reference.why: Dejados a nosotros mismos no podemos guardar la ley; nunca fue una escalera para subir a Dios.

mc.stem: 12. One great purpose of the law, the unit says, is to function as:
options: a mirror that shows our sin
mc.why: The law is a mirror that shows our sin and drives us to the cross; it diagnoses but cannot cure.

es_reference.stem: 12. Uno de los grandes propósitos de la ley, dice la unidad, es funcionar como:
options: una escalera para subir a Dios
un espejo que muestra nuestro pecado
es_reference.why: La ley es un espejo que muestra nuestro pecado y nos lleva a la cruz; diagnostica pero no puede curar.

mc.stem: 13. The cure for our inability to keep the law is identified as:
mc.why: The law diagnoses; the gospel cures, satisfying its demand and paying its penalty in Christ.

es_reference.stem: 13. La cura para nuestra incapacidad de guardar la ley se identifica como:
es_reference.why: La ley diagnostica; el evangelio cura, satisfaciendo su exigencia y pagando su pena en Cristo.

mc.stem: 14. Galatians 5:22–23 calls love, joy, peace, and the rest the:
mc.why: They are the fruit of the Spirit, borne in a soul united to Christ, not the achievement of the flesh.

es_reference.stem: 14. Gálatas 5:22–23 llama al amor, el gozo, la paz y lo demás el:
es_reference.why: Son el fruto del Espíritu, llevado en un alma unida a Cristo, no el logro de la carne.

mc.stem: 15. The unit stresses “fruit” rather than “works” to show that holiness is:
options: borne as the life of the vine flows through us
mc.why: Fruit is not manufactured by gritted teeth; it is borne as the life of the vine flows through the branch.

es_reference.stem: 15. La unidad recalca «fruto» en vez de «obras» para mostrar que la santidad es:
options: llevada conforme la vida de la vid fluye a través de nosotros
es_reference.why: El fruto no lo fabrican los dientes apretados; se lleva conforme la vida de la vid fluye a través de la rama.

mc.stem: 16. The course's governing order, restated here, is:
options: grace and works as equal causes
law before gospel as a permanent rule
mc.why: Grace first, always first; we obey because we have been accepted, not in order to be accepted.

es_reference.stem: 16. El orden rector del curso, reafirmado aquí, es:
options: la gracia primero, luego la obediencia
la obediencia primero, luego la gracia
la gracia y las obras como causas iguales
la ley antes del evangelio como regla permanente
es_reference.why: La gracia primero, siempre primero; obedecemos porque hemos sido aceptados, no para ser aceptados.

mc.stem: 17. Getting the grace-and-obedience order backward produces:
options: either a Pharisee or a wreck
mc.why: Reverse the order and you produce either a Pharisee or a wreck, often both by turns.

es_reference.stem: 17. Invertir el orden de la gracia y la obediencia produce:
options: o un fariseo o una ruina
es_reference.why: Invierta el orden y producirá o un fariseo o una ruina, a menudo ambas cosas por turnos.

mc.stem: 18. The grammatical-historical method first asks:
options: how the verse confirms our preferences
what the human author meant to his original readers
how it can be applied today
mc.why: It humbly asks what the author, carried by the Spirit, meant to his original readers—then how it bears on us.

es_reference.stem: 18. El método gramatical-histórico pregunta primero:
options: cómo el versículo confirma nuestras preferencias
qué quiso decir el autor humano a sus lectores originales
es_reference.why: Pregunta humildemente qué quiso decir el autor, llevado por el Espíritu, a sus lectores originales — y luego cómo nos toca.

mc.stem: 19. To bend a text toward what we already wished to do is described as making it:
mc.why: To bend a verse toward our preferences is to make it a wax nose; the man who does so has used the Word, not honored it.

es_reference.stem: 19. Doblar un texto hacia lo que ya queríamos hacer se describe como hacerlo:
es_reference.why: Doblar un versículo hacia nuestras preferencias es hacerlo una nariz de cera; quien lo hace ha usado la Palabra, no la ha honrado.

mc.stem: 20. The Christian's verdict on virtue, duty, and consequence is to:
options: gather the truth in each and order it under God's revelation
choose one and reject the rest
mc.why: Each system borrows from the moral order God built; the Christian gathers the truth in each and orders it under God's revelation.

es_reference.stem: 20. El veredicto del cristiano sobre la virtud, el deber y la consecuencia es:
options: reúne la verdad que hay en cada uno y la ordena bajo la revelación de Dios
escoge uno y rechaza los demás
es_reference.why: Cada sistema toma prestado del orden moral que Dios edificó; el cristiano reúne la verdad de cada uno y la ordena bajo la revelación de Dios.

sa.prompt: 21. Explain why the holiness of God, not a rule He keeps, is the ground of all ethics.
sa.model: The ground of all ethics is the holiness of God—not a rule He keeps, but the very purity of who He is. When God says “Be holy, for I am holy,” the reason for the standard is not the needs of the community or the usefulness of holy living but the nature of God Himself. Goodness is therefore neither arbitrary nor a standard above God; it is His own character expressed. His commands are the overflow of His perfect nature, which is why ethics must begin with who God is rather than with us.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Explique por qué la santidad de Dios, no una regla que Él guarda, es el fundamento de toda ética.
es_reference.model: El fundamento de toda ética es la santidad de Dios — no una regla que Él guarda, sino la pureza misma de quien Él es. Cuando Dios dice «Sed santos, porque yo soy santo», la razón de la norma no son las necesidades de la comunidad ni la utilidad de la vida santa, sino la naturaleza de Dios mismo. Por tanto la bondad no es ni arbitraria ni una norma por encima de Dios; es su propio carácter expresado. Sus mandamientos son el desbordamiento de su naturaleza perfecta, y por eso la ética debe comenzar con quien Dios es y no con nosotros.

sa.prompt: 22. State the two ancient errors about why things are good, and the biblical answer between them.
sa.model: The first error says things are good merely because God arbitrarily commands them—so He could have called murder righteous—which makes God a tyrant and goodness a coin-flip. The second says things are good by a standard above God to which even He must bow, which makes God no longer God but a servant of a higher law. The biblical answer slices between them: a thing is good because it reflects the unchanging character of God. Goodness is neither arbitrary nor above Him; it is Him, expressed.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Exponga los dos errores antiguos sobre por qué las cosas son buenas, y la respuesta bíblica entre ellos.
es_reference.model: El primer error dice que las cosas son buenas meramente porque Dios arbitrariamente las manda — de modo que pudo haber llamado justo al homicidio — lo cual hace de Dios un tirano y de la bondad un volado. El segundo dice que las cosas son buenas por una norma por encima de Dios a la que aun Él debe doblegarse, lo cual hace que Dios ya no sea Dios sino siervo de una ley superior. La respuesta bíblica corta entre ambos: una cosa es buena porque refleja el carácter inmutable de Dios. La bondad no es ni arbitraria ni superior a Él; es Él, expresado.

sa.prompt: 23. Explain the imago Dei principle and why human worth is irreducible.
sa.model: Every human being is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and therefore possesses a worth that cannot be earned, diminished, or revoked. That worth does not rise and fall with a man's usefulness, health, morality, or agreement with us. It is irreducible because it is grounded not in him but in the God whose image he bears. This principle governs the sanctity of life, the treatment of the poor, and the discipline of the sinning brother.

es_reference.prompt: 23. Explique el principio de la imago Dei y por qué el valor humano es irreducible.
es_reference.model: Todo ser humano está hecho a imagen de Dios (Génesis 1:27), y por tanto posee un valor que no puede ganarse, disminuirse ni revocarse. Ese valor no sube ni baja con la utilidad, la salud, la moralidad o el acuerdo de un hombre con nosotros. Es irreducible porque está fundado no en él sino en el Dios cuya imagen lleva. Este principio gobierna la santidad de la vida, el trato del pobre y la disciplina del hermano que peca.

sa.prompt: 24. Distinguish the ceremonial, civil, and moral strands of the Law and say which abides and why.
sa.model: Conservative teachers distinguish three strands in the law of Moses: the ceremonial governed sacrifice and temple, the civil ordered the nation of Israel, and the moral expresses God's unchanging will. The ceremonial pointed forward to Christ and is fulfilled in Him; the civil was given to a particular nation in a particular time; but the moral law, rooted in God's own nature, abides. This is why the church still teaches the Ten Commandments and no longer offers lambs, and why collapsing the distinction causes much confusion.

es_reference.prompt: 24. Distinga las hebras ceremonial, civil y moral de la Ley y diga cuál permanece y por qué.
es_reference.model: Los maestros conservadores distinguen tres hebras en la ley de Moisés: la ceremonial regía el sacrificio y el templo, la civil ordenaba a la nación de Israel, y la moral expresa la voluntad inmutable de Dios. La ceremonial apuntaba adelante a Cristo y se cumple en Él; la civil fue dada a una nación particular en un tiempo particular; pero la ley moral, arraigada en la naturaleza misma de Dios, permanece. Por esto la iglesia aún enseña los Diez Mandamientos y ya no ofrece corderos, y borrar la distinción causa mucha confusión.

sa.prompt: 25. How does Christ “fulfill” the law in the Sermon on the Mount rather than abolish or soften it?
sa.model: Christ says plainly that He came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17). Far from softening it, He drives it inward to the heart: you have heard ‘do not murder,’ but I say do not nurse the anger that kills; ‘do not commit adultery,’ but do not harbor the lust that betrays. He takes the law off the surface of behavior and presses it into the thoughts and intents. This is progressive revelation at its summit—not a new and contradictory standard but the full unveiling of what the law always meant.

es_reference.prompt: 25. ¿Cómo «cumple» Cristo la ley en el Sermón del Monte en vez de abolirla o suavizarla?
es_reference.model: Cristo dice claramente que vino no para abrogar la ley sino para cumplirla (Mateo 5:17). Lejos de suavizarla, la impulsa hacia adentro, al corazón: habéis oído «no matarás», pero yo digo: no abriguéis la ira que mata; «no cometerás adulterio», pero no alberguéis la concupiscencia que traiciona. Toma la ley de la superficie de la conducta y la oprime hasta los pensamientos y las intenciones. Esto es la revelación progresiva en su cúspide — no una norma nueva y contradictoria sino el pleno develamiento de lo que la ley siempre significó.

sa.prompt: 26. Why can no one keep the law, and what is the law's purpose given that?
sa.model: Left to ourselves we cannot keep the law, for there is none righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10). The law was never given as a ladder to climb to God. One of its great purposes is to be a mirror that shows us our filth and drives us, despairing of ourselves, to the cross. The law diagnoses; it cannot cure. The cure is the gospel, in which the law's demand is satisfied and its penalty paid in Christ.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Por qué nadie puede guardar la ley, y cuál es el propósito de la ley dado eso?
es_reference.model: Dejados a nosotros mismos no podemos guardar la ley, pues no hay justo, ni aun uno (Romanos 3:10). La ley nunca fue dada como una escalera para subir a Dios. Uno de sus grandes propósitos es ser un espejo que nos muestra nuestra inmundicia y nos lleva, desesperados de nosotros mismos, a la cruz. La ley diagnostica; no puede curar. La cura es el evangelio, en el cual la exigencia de la ley queda satisfecha y su pena pagada en Cristo.

sa.prompt: 27. Explain why holiness is called the “fruit” of the Spirit rather than the “works” of the flesh.
sa.model: Holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, not the achievement of the flesh (Galatians 5:22–23). The word is deliberately ‘fruit,’ not ‘works.’ Fruit is not manufactured by the branch gritting its teeth; it is borne as the life of the vine flows through it. Christian character is grown, by the Spirit, in a soul united to Christ—which rescues ethics from being a grim exercise in willpower.

es_reference.prompt: 27. Explique por qué la santidad se llama el «fruto» del Espíritu y no las «obras» de la carne.
es_reference.model: La santidad es el fruto del Espíritu, no el logro de la carne (Gálatas 5:22–23). La palabra es deliberadamente «fruto», no «obras». El fruto no lo fabrica la rama apretando los dientes; se lleva conforme la vida de la vid fluye a través de ella. El carácter cristiano es cultivado, por el Espíritu, en un alma unida a Cristo — lo cual rescata a la ética de ser un sombrío ejercicio de fuerza de voluntad.

sa.prompt: 28. State the course's governing order of grace and obedience and what reversing it produces.
sa.model: The governing order is grace before obedience, and the course never reverses it. We do not obey in order to be accepted; we have been accepted, and therefore we obey, and the very power to obey is itself a gift. Get the order backward and you produce either a Pharisee or a wreck. Keep it straight and obedience becomes the glad response of a son to the Father who has already run down the road to embrace him.

es_reference.prompt: 28. Exponga el orden rector del curso sobre la gracia y la obediencia y qué produce invertirlo.
es_reference.model: El orden rector es la gracia antes de la obediencia, y el curso nunca lo invierte. No obedecemos para ser aceptados; hemos sido aceptados, y por tanto obedecemos, y el poder mismo para obedecer es un don. Invierta el orden y producirá o un fariseo o una ruina. Manténgalo derecho y la obediencia se vuelve la respuesta gozosa de un hijo al Padre que ya ha corrido por el camino para abrazarlo.

sa.prompt: 29. Describe the grammatical-historical method and the danger of making a text a “wax nose.”
sa.model: The grammatical-historical method is a humble practice: we ask what the human author, carried along by the Spirit, actually meant to his original readers in the ordinary sense of his words and the setting of his time—and only then how that abiding truth bears on us. We must not make the text a mirror for our preferences or a wax nose bent toward whatever we already wished to do. The pastor who proves his point by ripping a verse from its context has used the Word, not honored it. The rule of context is to read the verse in its paragraph, the paragraph in its book, and the book in the whole counsel of God.

es_reference.prompt: 29. Describa el método gramatical-histórico y el peligro de hacer del texto una «nariz de cera».
es_reference.model: El método gramatical-histórico es una práctica humilde: preguntamos qué quiso decir el autor humano, llevado por el Espíritu, a sus lectores originales en el sentido ordinario de sus palabras y el entorno de su tiempo — y solo entonces cómo esa verdad permanente nos toca. No debemos hacer del texto un espejo de nuestras preferencias ni una nariz de cera doblada hacia lo que ya queríamos hacer. El pastor que prueba su punto arrancando un versículo de su contexto ha usado la Palabra, no la ha honrado. La regla del contexto es leer el versículo en su párrafo, el párrafo en su libro y el libro en todo el consejo de Dios.

sa.prompt: 30. How should a Christian weigh the virtue, duty, and consequence systems of ethics?
sa.model: The philosophers largely sort into three families: those who locate the good in character (virtue), in duty and rule (deontology), and in consequences (utilitarianism). Each has hold of something real, because each borrows from the moral order God actually built—Scripture cares about character, duty, and consequences alike. The failure of each is not that it sees nothing true but that it tears its one fragment loose from God and makes it carry the whole weight alone. The Christian does not choose one and reject the rest; he gathers the truth in each and orders all of it under the authority of God's revelation.

es_reference.prompt: 30. ¿Cómo debe el cristiano sopesar los sistemas éticos de la virtud, el deber y la consecuencia?
es_reference.model: Los filósofos se clasifican en gran medida en tres familias: los que ubican el bien en el carácter (virtud), en el deber y la regla (deontología), y en las consecuencias (utilitarismo). Cada una tiene asida algo real, porque cada una toma prestado del orden moral que Dios edificó — la Escritura se preocupa por el carácter, el deber y las consecuencias por igual. El fracaso de cada una no es que no vea nada verdadero sino que arranca su único fragmento de Dios y lo hace cargar solo todo el peso. El cristiano no escoge una y rechaza las demás; reúne la verdad de cada una y la ordena bajo la autoridad de la revelación de Dios.
